assumptions: The prospective business does not itself perform regulated market functions without the required authorization or licensed partner.
Installer relationships and customer data are available only through explicit consent-based contracts.
The initial 80,000 PLN funds analytics and a narrow integration pilot rather than battery assets.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A signed aggregator sandbox, verified Polish revenue stack and minimum portfolio size, capacity reservations from 20-50 compatible sites, measured net revenue per site, dispatch reliability, override behavior, settlement timing, and conservative unit economics.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Small flexible assets require contractual aggregation, verified baselines, and settlement access before their fragmented capacity can be monetized.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Lower bills and flexibility revenue are measurable outcomes, but Polish revenue stacks, site-level value, and SME willingness to surrender dispatch rights are unknown.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Recurring platform and performance revenue could scale, but partner shares, telemetry, integrations, settlement lag, field support, and 24-36 month payback make economics fragile.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Compatible SMEs recruited through installers are a coherent beachhead, but the available near-term Polish portfolio and minimum viable aggregation scale are not established.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: A vendor-neutral pool could occupy a niche, yet licensed aggregators, utilities, and OEMs control settlement, supply relationships, or hardware and can disintermediate it.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A functioning pool can extend across batteries, EV chargers, controllable loads, installers, regions, and additional energy-market revenue streams.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Contracted capacity and dispatch-response history can compound, but no capacity rights exist and customer overrides or partner dependence can weaken the moat.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Vendor-neutral orchestration may unlock otherwise inaccessible value, but the incremental economics versus OEM or utility offerings are unproven.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: EU policy favors storage, demand response, and active participation, although Polish implementation and monetization readiness remain uncertain.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Installers offer a plausible enrollment channel, but no consented customer access, signed distribution, aggregator relationship, or site CAC is available.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The concept requires device integrations, reliable baselines, cybersecurity, customer contracts, and licensed market access, exceeding what AI alone or a part-time founder can solve.

highest_value_structural_change: Obtain a contractual white-label role with a licensed aggregator that fixes market access, settlement economics, customer ownership boundaries, and protection against disintermediation.
main_structural_strength: If contractual capacity is secured, recurring dispatch data and portfolio density can create a scalable coordination asset with broad expansion options.
primary_score_limiter: The business lacks control of every essential rail—devices, dispatch rights, customer relationships, metering, market access, and settlement.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Polish market-access rules may not support small portfolios, while hardware fragmentation and customer overrides can destroy the dispatch reliability required for revenue.
